facts.text: In 1818 the Black Ball Line started the first regular fleet of sailing packets between New York and Liverpool.
The packets left and arrived on a fixed schedule, so travelers could plan their movements with fair certainty.
The packets were built for safety, comfort and cargo space rather than speed.
For a sailing packet, a crossing of 18 or 20 days counted as a good passage.
In 1838 the steamships Sirius and Great Western sailed from Britain to New York; Sirius took 17.5 days and the Great Western 15 days.
In 1850 the American steamship Atlantic crossed from New York to Liverpool in 10 days and 16 hours.
Before the cable, news crossed the Atlantic only as fast as the fastest ship could sail.
Cyrus Field began the transatlantic cable project in 1854.
Cables were lost or broke in earlier attempts before the cable was completed on August 5, 1858.
Queen Victoria's 98-word message to President James Buchanan took 17 hours to send over the 1858 cable.
facts.note: s2 寫 more than 16 hours、不到 100 字；題目採 s3 的 17 小時、98 字

facts.text: The first cable was very slow and could carry only a few words per hour.
Hoping to make the weak, slow signals travel faster, the chief electrician raised the voltage to 2,000 volts.
After about a month of use, the insulation of the 1858 cable burned through off the coast of Ireland and the cable stopped working.
An 1861 British inquiry blamed the failure on poor manufacture and on raising the voltage to speed up the signals.
The American Civil War held up the project; a new cable broke in 1865, and a working cable was laid in 1866.
The 1866 cable was laid by the Great Eastern, the largest ship of its day, which had failed as a passenger ship because it burned too much fuel.
The 1865–1866 cable was about one inch thick, twice as thick as the half-inch early cables, and it worked at low voltage.
The 1866 cable could carry 6 to 8 words per minute.
With the working cable, news that would have taken about 12 days by ship crossed between Europe and North America in minutes.
On December 12, 1901, at St. John's, Newfoundland, Marconi picked up a radio signal sent from England, using an antenna held up by a kite.
On January 18, 1903, the first public two-way wireless exchange between America and Europe carried messages between President Theodore Roosevelt and King Edward VII.
The Cape Cod wireless station sent messages between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m., when conditions in the air were best.
Wireless messages from the station cost 50 cents a word, and skilled operators sent about 17 words per minute.
Derived: 17 words per minute is more than twice the 1866 cable's top speed of 8 words per minute (2 × 8 = 16).
Derived: the Great Western's 15-day crossing was not even a third shorter than a good 18–20 day packet passage, far from half the time.
Telstar 1 was launched on July 10, 1962, and within hours it relayed the first live television pictures across the Atlantic, to France.
Telstar could relay broadcasts for only about 18 minutes at a time, while its orbit carried it over the Atlantic.
In 1953 film of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation had to be flown to New York, because live television could not yet cross the ocean.
Undersea cables now carry about 98 percent of the world's information.

facts.text: From the first regular packet line in 1818 to Telstar in 1962 is 144 years, nearly a century and a half.
